Gnädigster Herr
Mein erſter Vorſaz war, Ewr Hochfürſtl. Durchlaucht durchaus keine Audiosa mehr
zu melden, und Dinge die nicht mehr zu andern wären ihren Gang gehen zu laßen.
Nothgedrungen aber muß ich diesen Vorsazz aufgeben und Hochstderoselbe Hülfe recta
mirn — die Sache ist diese.
Ehe ich hieher gieng erhielt ich das Lub Lili A beigebogene Schreiben des v. Bornstadt
in Posen. Ich hätte von dem Verfaßer keine gute Meinung und suchte ihm dadurch
zu demüthigen, daß ich dh. p. Glenck ein bloßes Recipisse geben lies, da es in Sachen
Sr Durch ein Schreiben d. po Bomstadt eingegangen wäre, worüber er als General
Mandatarius ihm bescheiden würde.
Ich suchte u Person als dann noch den Melzer und den Pre: Braunschuſung zu gewinnen
ein alles aufzubieten, daß die Berliner Verfügung aufrecht erhalten und die
Gelder deponirt werden mögten beſonders aber daß Broniewski gleich exmittirt
werden mögte. Mann versprach mir dies und ich reisete allen in der Nacht
hierher nach Betsche, ſchickte ſogleich einen reitenden Boten nach Franckfurth
und beſtellte Meyer Bernhard und Conſorten hier her. Beigehende Abſchrift
Lub B beſagt das weitere.
Nach dieser Expedition bis ich die Deputirten welche in Breslau waren rußen
äußerst befremdend war es mich daß keiner erscheinen wolte, endlich er
fuhr ich daß die Leute aufgehögt waren vom Kauf zurückzutreten,
Ich suchte den Grund zu erforschen, und höhrte zu meinen Schrecken, daß der Rochlitz
die Leute die Köpfe verwirre und ſie drohe, alles zu zerreißen, weil er um
sein Schwager Klein einen Contract in Händen hätte nach welchen sie das Vor-

Vorwerk Abre und den grösten Theil der Waldung abnehmen würden.
Der Justiz Burge Meister Metzig, der als Beistand der Gemeinde ernannt
ist, erklärte mir endlich gerade hin, daß ihm H. B. v. Glenck angelegen die
ganze Verhandlung in Breslau zu zureichten, daß er große Forderung
habe die er geltend machen würde, und daß er Henck, wenn er der
Metzig mit ihm halten wolle, sehr erkenntlich sein würde.
Er Metzig erklärte ferner, daß er zwar sehe daß man Ewr Durchlau¬
prellen wolle, daß er aber als Beistand der Gemeinden darauf bei
stehen müße.

Schreiben des v. Bornstädt, erfuhr auch noch von mehreren Einsaßen daß

zu zernichten, er wolte ſie alle davor glücklich machen
Warum Glenck dies thut bleibt im Rathsel.
Ich erwartete übrigens seine und Wunsters Ankunft-Glenck erfolgte vor
gestern. Ich war bemüht alles auf das gelindeste zu erforschen habe aber
nichts weiter von ihm heraus gebracht, daß er nichts wiße indem
ihm die Pappiere mangelten, auf die Frage wo der zwischen ihm und
dem Leixner geschloßene Contract sey, antwortet er, daß solchen
der Lieut: v Brandenstein hinter sich habe, und auf sein Gut oder das
Geld dafür dringen würde.

beigehendes Schreiben des v Bornstädt sub d aber beweis daß Glenck mir belogen und
daß der Contract bereits an, Kaufmann Klein einen Vetter des Röcklis
Cedirt sey. Noch zweifelte ich und suchte alles mit den Leuten aufs Beste
zu arangiren, bis ich beigehendes Billet sub C von Meyer Bernhard
erhielt. Dies veranlaßt mich diese Estaffette schleunig an Ewr Durchlaucht
zu senden.
Sowohl die Gemeinden, als die Franckfartler bestehen darauf daß dieser
zwischen Leixner und den Herrn v. Brandenstein geschloßene Contract
vor allen Dingen herbey geſchaft, um völlig Cassirt werde.

tract heraus giebt.

Extaffitte ſchreiben daß er ſofort dieſe ſamtl Pappiere heraus giebt, und
daß so wohl er als Herr v Brandenstein ſich wegen der Aufhebung beide
Contracte gerichtl. reverirn, daß sie weiter nichts von die Franckfurther
herren, — oder von die Betecher Gründe praetendiren können, oder mögen.
v Brandenstein, der schwerlich von alle die Drehereien des H. Glenck was wißen
mag, wird den Reversch dorten gewis gleich ausſtellen, und ich bitte unterthänig
daß Ewr Durchlaucht diesen jungen Mann, der wohl an der Sache ganz unsthuldig

sein mag, höchst Ihre Gnade nicht zu entziehen. Ich werde auch dafür in meinen Erster
nicht ermüden.

Ja auf das eiligste zur Estaffette hier her zu senden. Den sonsten kan ich nichts
mit den Leuten abmachen.

Zurück schaft um selbigen nebst den Locietrets Contract zurük giebt und

Ich hätte Ewer Durchl. gerne mit dieser Sache verschont. Ich komme aber anders
nicht durch, den die Leute bestehen darauf.
Mit Bomstadt sieht alles schrecklich verworren aus Glenck Rochlitz [Werleben?]
Bornſtädt, und wie das Gesindel alles heißt, haben ſich ſtets wie die
Keßelflicker unter Ewr Durchlaucht Augen gezänckt, im Grunde
aber haben sie alle in brüderlicher Eintracht betrogen, daß jedem die
Haare zu Berge stehen. Ewr Durchlaucht wäre es stets den sie alle
gerne reine ausgeplündert hätte.
Der Wald ist ganz ruinirt und was die Diebe noch ein Jahrhier ge¬
Laußet hätte, so waren die ſchönen Güter nicht 50000 mehr werth –
Jezt bin ich bemüht den Bornstädt so recht solide zu überflügeln.
Er ſchien Gebrauch von den Verkauf am der Unterthanen zu machen.

gemachter Sache ſezzen laßen. Da werde ich den wohl mit den Helden
fertig werden – Schändlich ist es mir daß solche infamun in dem
Acten vorkommen, so sagt der Bornstadt zu Beispiel Bey

anderer Pächter verſprach ihn nach Jahres Frist mehr darum wolte er
mich vertreiben, um wieder 600 Rthl zu erpreßen.
Unwahr, sagt er weiter, muß er doch wohl sein, daß der Herr
Fürst, wie Glenck sich rühmt, um solche Prelliren weis¬
den der Fürst hatt doch den Auf des erhabensten grösten Mannes und Men¬
sehen freundes
Rasend mögte ich werden wenn ich so was vor Augen bekomme, und
ich kan weiter nichts wünschen als alle diese schmuggige Dinge zu beseitigen
und dergestalt aus der Welt zu ſchaffen, daß Ewr Durchlaucht keinen Ver
dens mehr haben.

Bornstädt, wan er Betschen für 200000 Rthl verkaufen hilft, 1000 stück
frid: Sor zugesagt. Glenck hat dies hier vor dem Metzig bestätiget.

ihm abfinden? Geruhen Sie gnädigster Fürst mir desfals eine
Weisung zu gebe.
Die Pacht Sache würde ich rechtens abmachen, und bey Gott nichts ver¬
ſchneben, aber in der Geſchichte kan ich ohne Ewr Durchl. Befehl nichts
weiter thun. Generals, um Gott weis welche Menschen alle in

translation.en:
Most Serene Prince

Most gracious Lord, My first resolve was to report no further odious matters to Your Most Serene Highness, and to let things which could no longer be altered take their course. But of necessity I must abandon this resolve and [uncertain: implore] Your Highness's help directly — the matter is this.

Before I came here I received the letter of von Bornstädt in Posen enclosed under Lit. A. I had no good opinion of the writer and sought to humble him by having a bare acknowledgement of receipt given through Glenck, since a letter from Bornstädt had come in concerning His Serene Highness's affairs, upon which he, as general mandatary, would advise him.

I then sought further to win over in person Melzer and the [uncertain: Pre: Braunschuſung] and to bring everything to bear so that the Berlin decree might be upheld and the monies deposited, but above all that Broniewski might be evicted at once. This was promised me, and I travelled all through the night here to Betsche, at once despatched a mounted messenger to Frankfurt an der Oder and summoned Meyer Bernhard and associates here. The enclosed Copy Lit. B tells the rest.

After this despatch I [uncertain: summoned] the deputies who were in Breslau; it was exceedingly strange to me that none of them would appear. At last I learned that the people had been incited to withdraw from the purchase. I sought to discover the ground of it, and heard to my horror that Rochlitz was confusing the people's heads and threatening them, that he would tear the whole thing apart, because through his brother-in-law Klein he had a contract in hand under which they would take away the

demesne farm [uncertain: Abre] and the greater part of the woodland. The justice-burgomaster Metzig, who is appointed as counsel to the community, at last declared to me outright that Councillor von Glenck was concerned to direct the whole negotiation to Breslau, that he had large claims which he would enforce, and that he, Glenck, would be very grateful to him, Metzig, if he would side with him. Metzig further declared that he indeed saw that Your Serene Highness was to be cheated, but that as counsel to the communities he must insist upon it,

first, that this matter be wholly cleared up, and secondly, that everything with Councillor von Bornstädt must first be settled; before that the communities can pay no money and enter into nothing. After this sad experience I received the letter of von Bornstädt enclosed under Lit. C, and learned further from several residents that

Councillor Glenck had requested them to withdraw from the contract and to annul it, saying he would make them all happy in return. Why Glenck does this remains a riddle.

For the rest I awaited his and Wunster's arrival — Glenck arrived the day before yesterday. I took pains to sound out everything in the gentlest manner, but got nothing further out of him than that he knew nothing, since he lacked the papers; to the question where the contract concluded between him and Leixner might be, he answers that Lieutenant von Brandenstein has it in his keeping, and would press for his estate or the money for it.

But the enclosed letter of von Bornstädt sub d proves that Glenck lied to me and that the contract has already been ceded to the merchant Klein, a cousin of Rochlitz. Still I doubted, and sought to arrange everything with the people for the best, until I received the enclosed note sub C from Meyer Bernhard. This moves me to send this express courier in haste to Your Serene Highness.

Both the communities and the Frankfurt men insist that this contract concluded between Leixner and Herr von Brandenstein be above all things produced, so that it may be wholly cancelled. Secondly, Bernhard and Leixner will pay not one Groschen further until Glenck hands over the partnership contract concluded between them.

Thirdly, the communities insist that everything be settled with Bornstädt; before that they will agree to nothing further. My counsel and request is this, that Your Most Serene Highness write to Glenck by express courier that he hand over all these papers at once, and that both he and Herr von Brandenstein give a judicial written undertaking as to the annulment of both contracts, that they can or may claim nothing further from the Frankfurt gentlemen — or from the Betsche lands. Von Brandenstein, who can hardly know anything of all Councillor Glenck's twistings, will certainly issue the written undertaking there at once, and I most humbly beg that Your Serene Highness may not withdraw your grace from this young man, who may well be entirely innocent

in the matter. Nor shall I tire in my [uncertain: endeavour] on his behalf.

May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send me the written undertaking from Herr von Brandenstein here with all speed by the express courier. For otherwise I can settle nothing with the people.

But let Your Highness command Glenck to fetch back the ceded contract here at once, to return it together with the partnership contract, and to renounce all claims judicially.

I would gladly have spared Your Serene Highness this business. But I cannot get through otherwise, for the people insist upon it.

With Bornstädt everything looks frightfully tangled. Glenck, Rochlitz, [uncertain: Werleben], Bornstädt, and whatever else the rabble are called, have constantly squabbled like tinkers before Your Serene Highness's eyes, but at bottom they have all cheated in brotherly concord, enough to make anyone's hair stand on end. It was always Your Serene Highness whom they would all gladly have plundered clean.

The wood is wholly ruined, and had the thieves gone on here another year, the fine estates would not have been worth 50000 any longer. — Now I am at pains to outflank Bornstädt really soundly. He seemed to be making use of the sale to the subjects; but these I have brought so far that, against my guarantee, they will let him be until the matter is concluded. Then I shall doubtless finish with the hero. — It is shameful to me that such infamies occur in the files; thus Bornstädt says for example: On

entering upon my lease I had to lay out 500 Rthl to Glenck as a broker's fee; another tenant promised him more after a year's term, and for that reason he wished to drive me out, so as to extort 600 Rthl again. It must surely be untrue, he says further, that the Prince, as Glenck boasts of himself, knows of such cheating, for the Prince has after all the reputation of the most exalted, greatest man and friend of mankind. I could go mad when such a thing comes before my eyes, and I can wish nothing further than to put aside all these squalid matters and so to clear them out of the world that Your Serene Highness may have no more [uncertain: vexation].

What torments me most at present is this — Your Serene Highness promised Bornstädt 1000 pieces of Friedrichsd'or if he helps to sell Betsche for 200000 Rthl. Glenck has confirmed this here before Metzig. What am I, poor man, now to answer to that? The fellow tenders the oath on this point to Your Serene Highness, to Glenck and to Rochlitz. What am I to answer the fellow to this, and with what am I to settle with him? Be pleased, most gracious Prince, to give me an instruction in the matter.

The lease business I would settle lawfully, and by God give nothing away, but in this affair I can do nothing further without Your Serene Highness's command. Generals, and God knows what people, all take an interest on behalf of the wretched creature and his wife, who seems to be a true [uncertain: kantigen]

to be; therefore I wish to be rid of the wretched B. with good manners.

As to the timber contracts it looks just as [uncertain: dreadful] — for as many as there are, they belong to Rochlitz under other names. The name-bearers are now all crying out that they want no money but the sums of timber fixed in the contracts. This is now to be another motive for annulling the purchase with the subjects. But here I shall speak loudly with the rogues. For the whole communities will come forward and loudly prove the villains' infamies. — Your Serene Highness will be astonished at all the knaveries.

This very moment I learn of a new intrigue of Glenck's. I had, as said before, brought Meyer Bernhard so far that he meant to be in Posen on the 29th in the evening or the 30th early with the 66000 Rthl. At this moment Wünster tells me that Glenck has talked Meyer Bernhard into not paying the money on the 29th, but going to Breslau and asking Your Serene Highness what he should do — for it would not be necessary before the 2nd of August that the money be paid over to Broniewski.

The Jew now twists again, says he would do this, that he has so many claims upon Your Serene Highness. We all sit here now like fools. — It is more than too bad.

what these people permit themselves. — As to the Kaemener and Kulmner dismemberment I can likewise do nothing for the present. For Glenck has already betrayed everything to him (of which the letter enclosed under Lit. F is proof), everything, so as to earn something. O God! what shameful people are these? I shall see what the Jew means to do; if he insists on the journey to Breslau, then I shall only see how I may get half-way finished with the subjects here, and shall come there too at that time; but then I beg Your Serene Highness also, most heartily, to work over all these B. really harshly, so that they may once come to be afraid and drop the damned machinations. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's

May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send the express courier with all the papers to Posen to old Reinhardt. If I can still turn everything about, I shall be there — if not, then he must send them to me here. Ah, it is true hellish torment to bring these people to reason. The letter to my daughter I most submissively beg to have delivered, and if anything has come in there from South Prussia etc., to let it go with me by the express courier. Betsche, the 26th of July

1804

faithful, humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld

I took pains to sound out everything in the gentlest manner, but got nothing further out of him than that he knew nothing, since he lacked the papers; to the question where the contract concluded between him and Leixner might be, he answers that Lieutenant von Brandenstein has it in his keeping, and would press for his estate or the money for it.

But the enclosed letter of von Bornstädt sub d proves that Glenck lied to me and that the contract has already been ceded to the merchant Klein, a cousin of Rochlitz. Still I doubted, and sought to arrange everything with the people for the best, until I received the enclosed note sub C from Meyer Bernhard. This moves me to send this express courier in haste to Your Serene Highness.

Both the communities and the Frankfurt men insist that this contract concluded between Leixner and Herr von Brandenstein be above all things produced, so that it may be wholly cancelled. Secondly, Bernhard and Leixner will pay not one Groschen further until Glenck hands over the partnership contract concluded between them.

Thirdly, the communities insist that everything be settled with Bornstädt; before that they will agree to nothing further. My counsel and request is this, that Your Most Serene Highness write to Glenck by express courier that he hand over all these papers at once, and that both he and Herr von Brandenstein give a judicial written undertaking as to the annulment of both contracts, that they can or may claim nothing further from the Frankfurt gentlemen — or from the Betsche lands. Von Brandenstein, who can hardly know anything of all Councillor Glenck's twistings, will certainly issue the written undertaking there at once, and I most humbly beg that Your Serene Highness may not withdraw your grace from this young man, who may well be entirely innocent

in the matter. Nor shall I tire in my [uncertain: endeavour] on his behalf.

May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send me the written undertaking from Herr von Brandenstein here with all speed by the express courier. For otherwise I can settle nothing with the people.

But let Your Highness command Glenck to fetch back the ceded contract here at once, to return it together with the partnership contract, and to renounce all claims judicially.

I would gladly have spared Your Serene Highness this business. But I cannot get through otherwise, for the people insist upon it.

With Bornstädt everything looks frightfully tangled. Glenck, Rochlitz, [uncertain: Werleben], Bornstädt, and whatever else the rabble are called, have constantly squabbled like tinkers before Your Serene Highness's eyes, but at bottom they have all cheated in brotherly concord, enough to make anyone's hair stand on end. It was always Your Serene Highness whom they would all gladly have plundered clean.

The wood is wholly ruined, and had the thieves gone on here another year, the fine estates would not have been worth 50000 any longer. — Now I am at pains to outflank Bornstädt really soundly. He seemed to be making use of the sale to the subjects; but these I have brought so far that, against my guarantee, they will let him be until the matter is concluded. Then I shall doubtless finish with the hero. — It is shameful to me that such infamies occur in the files; thus Bornstädt says for example: On

entering upon my lease I had to lay out 500 Rthl to Glenck as a broker's fee; another tenant promised him more after a year's term, and for that reason he wished to drive me out, so as to extort 600 Rthl again. It must surely be untrue, he says further, that the Prince, as Glenck boasts of himself, knows of such cheating, for the Prince has after all the reputation of the most exalted, greatest man and friend of mankind. I could go mad when such a thing comes before my eyes, and I can wish nothing further than to put aside all these squalid matters and so to clear them out of the world that Your Serene Highness may have no more [uncertain: vexation].

What torments me most at present is this — Your Serene Highness promised Bornstädt 1000 pieces of Friedrichsd'or if he helps to sell Betsche for 200000 Rthl. Glenck has confirmed this here before Metzig. What am I, poor man, now to answer to that? The fellow tenders the oath on this point to Your Serene Highness, to Glenck and to Rochlitz. What am I to answer the fellow to this, and with what am I to settle with him? Be pleased, most gracious Prince, to give me an instruction in the matter.

The lease business I would settle lawfully, and by God give nothing away, but in this affair I can do nothing further without Your Serene Highness's command. Generals, and God knows what people, all take an interest on behalf of the wretched creature and his wife, who seems to be a true [uncertain: kantigen]

to be; therefore I wish to be rid of the wretched B. with good manners.

As to the timber contracts it looks just as [uncertain: dreadful] — for as many as there are, they belong to Rochlitz under other names. The name-bearers are now all crying out that they want no money but the sums of timber fixed in the contracts. This is now to be another motive for annulling the purchase with the subjects. But here I shall speak loudly with the rogues. For the whole communities will come forward and loudly prove the villains' infamies. — Your Serene Highness will be astonished at all the knaveries.

This very moment I learn of a new intrigue of Glenck's. I had, as said before, brought Meyer Bernhard so far that he meant to be in Posen on the 29th in the evening or the 30th early with the 66000 Rthl. At this moment Wünster tells me that Glenck has talked Meyer Bernhard into not paying the money on the 29th, but going to Breslau and asking Your Serene Highness what he should do — for it would not be necessary before the 2nd of August that the money be paid over to Broniewski.

The Jew now twists again, says he would do this, that he has so many claims upon Your Serene Highness. We all sit here now like fools. — It is more than too bad.

For Glenck has already betrayed everything to him (of which the letter enclosed under Lit. F is proof), everything, so as to earn something. O God! what shameful people are these? I shall see what the Jew means to do; if he insists on the journey to Breslau, then I shall only see how I may get half-way finished with the subjects here, and shall come there too at that time; but then I beg Your Serene Highness also, most heartily, to work over all these B. really harshly, so that they may once come to be afraid and drop the damned machinations. In deepest reverence I remain, until death, Your Most Serene Highness's

May Your Most Serene Highness be pleased to send the express courier with all the papers to Posen to old Reinhardt. If I can still turn everything about, I shall be there — if not, then he must send them to me here. Ah, it is true hellish torment to bring these people to reason. The letter to my daughter I most submissively beg to have delivered, and if anything has come in there from South Prussia etc., to let it go with me by the express courier. Betsche, the 26th of July

1804

faithful, humble and obedient servant

von Triebenfeld
summary_en: Reports the collapse of the Betsche sale to the peasant communes: Glenck is accused of urging the villagers to withdraw, of lying about the contract with Leixner (in fact ceded to the merchant Klein, cousin of Rochlitz), and of persuading Meyer Bernhard to delay paying 66000 Rthl at Posen. Encloses letters from v. Bornstädt (who claims a promised 1000 Friedrichsd'or for selling Betschen at 200000 Rthl and alleges a 500 Rthl proxenticium to Glenck), asks for express orders compelling Glenck and Lieut. v. Brandenstein to surrender and judicially cancel both contracts, and complains of ruined woodland and fraudulent timber contracts.
summary_de: Bericht über die gefährdete Veräußerung von Betsche: Glenck habe die Gemeinden zum Rücktritt vom Kaufvertrag aufgestachelt, den mit Leixner geschlossenen Contract über Klein, einen Verwandten des Rochlitz, cediert und leugne dies; Justizbürgermeister Metzig und v. Bornstädt (Beilagen A–F) bestätigten die Umtriebe. Gefordert werden fürstliche Befehle per Estafette an Glenck und Lieut. v. Brandenstein zur Herausgabe und gerichtlichen Cassation beider Contracte sowie des Societätsvertrags. Meyer Bernhard verzögere die Zahlung der 66000 Rthl in Posen; Bornstädt berufe sich auf zugesagte 1000 Fried:d'or bei Verkauf für 200000 Rthl; der Wald sei ruiniert.
